Framework Documentation
The Adaptive Convexity Framework

Part 2 of 6 · ≈ 15 min read · In pictures · 9 exhibits →

Lineage & Macro Thesis

Framework Lineage

The intellectual foundations, thesis-agnostic.

Part 1 argued that the traditional playbook is failing. Part 2 names where the replacement comes from: four thinkers whose principles hold whatever is in play. They shape how the framework defines risk, sizes conviction, reads the feedback between prices and fundamentals, and thinks about time.

Keep two layers apart. The lineage supplies the method: how to think about risk, conviction, sizing and survival. The macro thesis supplies the application: where structural forces are directing capital now. The method persists across regimes, and the application changes with them. A new thesis can retune the framework’s parameters within fixed bounds (in the dashboard, a thesis profile moves each component weight by at most 10 percentage points, as of September 2026), but it never rewrites the method.

So before any macro thesis is allowed to matter, the method decides how risk, evidence and invalidation will be handled.

The method starts with the thinker who put survival ahead of everything else.

Antifragile · The Black Swan · Fooled by Randomness

Nassim Nicholas Taleb: Antifragility & ruin avoidance

Taleb contributes three observations: is nonlinear, ruin is irreversible, and the shape of a payoff matters more than the accuracy of a forecast. Traditional portfolio theory measures risk as standard deviation, which counts a gain and a loss of the same size alike. That is convenient mathematics and an incomplete account of survival: two portfolios can share the same volatility and face very different odds of living through it.

His pairs extreme safety with extreme and skips the middle. In The Black Swan he puts 85 to 90 percent in instruments as safe as Treasury bills and 10 to 15 percent in highly speculative bets. The framework keeps his priorities and loosens his proportions: its safe end is income-producing rather than Treasury bills, and Bitcoin and the growth positions carry the convexity. It also puts volatility to work instead of minimizing it: turns it into tax savings, read it as a signal, and turn it into attention. Taleb argued in 2021 that Bitcoin had failed as a currency. The framework uses his tools (barbells, convex payoffs, ruin avoidance) on a Bitcoin holding sized and paced under Part 3’s rules, and leaves his verdict on the asset to him.

Synthesis

  • Failure mode addressed. Mean-variance optimization turns fragile when correlations break and assets that looked balanced fall together.
  • Principle extracted. Build for survival first, optionality second and optimization third. Accept high volatility in the convex positions, because the safe ones keep the portfolio alive.
  • Framework implementation. A barbell-style structure; CIS Risk and Fragility scoring of how each position survives stress (balance sheet, business model, sensitivity to market factors, tail exposure); correlation across holdings watched at the portfolio level (Part 5); and tripwires that turn volatility into signals someone has to act on.

The framework therefore treats ruin as a boundary condition, not as one risk input among many.

Survival only keeps you in the game. Once the portfolio is built to survive, the next question is how boldly to build on it, and that is Druckenmiller’s territory.

The New Market Wizards · Lost Tree Club speech, 2015

Stanley Druckenmiller: Conviction & asymmetric positioning

Druckenmiller is known for concentration paired with close monitoring. In a 2015 talk at the Lost Tree Club he used an old line for it, one he has credited to Mark Twain: “put all your eggs in one basket and then watch the basket very carefully.” Spread capital across everything and you get something close to the average. Concentrate where conviction is real, watch it closely, and asymmetric outcomes become possible.

In The New Market Wizards he credits the rule behind it to George Soros: “The way to build long-term returns is through preservation of capital and home runs.” Small losses keep the capital intact, and a few large, high-conviction wins do most of the compounding. In the same interview he calls Soros “the best loss-taker I’ve ever seen.” The pattern is to concentrate when conviction is high and cut promptly when the reason for owning something breaks, which inverts the usual instruction to stay diversified at all times.

Synthesis

  • Failure mode addressed. Equal weights across 50 or more positions dilute conviction and make a meaningful asymmetric outcome unlikely.
  • Principle extracted. Size should follow the depth of conviction, and a broken reason to own something calls for a prompt exit.
  • Framework implementation. CIS (Part 6) turns conviction into a score. The score selects the posture-specific sizing band: 70 or above supports core sizing, 60 to 69 standard sizing, and 50 to 59 starter sizing. CIS below 50 removes allocation eligibility. Concentration stays inside the per-position and portfolio limits of Part 5, and at 50 and above, exits are governed by posture rules, tripwires and thesis evidence, not by the score band alone.

Conviction helps only when the exit standard is set before the position becomes emotional.

Conviction and exits both assume the market is something you read. Soros adds that the market reads you back.

The Alchemy of Finance

George Soros: Reflexivity & regime feedback loops

Soros’s theory of reflexivity challenges a central assumption of equilibrium economics: that prices passively reflect fundamentals. In his account they also shape them. Beliefs move prices, prices change fundamentals, and the new fundamentals then confirm or undercut the beliefs, in cycles that can reinforce or defeat themselves. Markets can stay away from equilibrium for a long time.

The loops get stronger during regime transitions. Rising prices attract capital; capital can improve fundamentals through cheaper financing, talent and credibility; better fundamentals seem to justify higher prices, until some constraint breaks the cycle. The same mechanism runs through policy. Under , debt issuance encourages monetary accommodation, accommodation supports asset prices, and the wealth effect keeps more spending politically feasible. That is : markets and policymakers reacting to each other in turn. Bitcoin adoption can follow a similar loop.

Synthesis

  • Failure mode addressed. Linear cause-and-effect models that assume price passively reflects value misjudge how large moves get and how long they last.
  • Principle extracted. Feedback loops gain influence during transitions. Watch for reflexive reinforcement (extension) and reflexive reversal (exit). Price is a participant in the system as well as an observer.
  • Framework implementation. Tripwires watch for signs of reflexive reversal. Sizing allows for loops that run further than looks rational. Flows and liquidity rank alongside fundamentals, and a thesis is invalidated fast when the feedback reverses.

The loop below runs in both directions: the chain that builds a boom can also unwind it.

Reflexive loops play out over months and years. Edelman works on a much longer clock: a saver’s whole life, where small edges in how money is held compound into large differences.

The Truth About Your Future · The Truth About Crypto

Ric Edelman: Longevity horizon

Edelman argues that advances in medicine and technology will make living to 100 far more common. For scale, U.S. life expectancy at birth was 79.0 years in 2024, and a 65-year-old could expect about 20 more (CDC). But a saver who starts at 25 and lives to 95 has a 70-year horizon, and over 60 to 80 years the meaning of “prudent” changes. That horizon is why the framework’s emphasis on convexity and on tax treatment holds whatever the macro thesis.

The framework draws the tax consequence: over 60 years, if gains are realized along the way, the gap between taxable and tax-free growth can exceed what security selection adds. The same horizon changes how small convex positions look. One that seems risky over 10 years can matter more over 60, because the cost of missing asymmetric upside compounds too. Edelman has put numbers on this for crypto. His published guidance moved from as little as 1 percent (The Truth About Crypto, 2022) to 10 to 40 percent in June 2025: 10 for conservative, 25 for moderate and 40 for aggressive investors. His moderate mix, 50 percent stocks, 25 percent bonds and 25 percent crypto, drops 60/40 as the default. The framework adopts neither figure; Part 3 sets its own ranges for Bitcoin.

Synthesis

  • Failure mode addressed. Plans built for a shorter life than the saver may live, 60/40 held as a default rather than chosen, and tax treatment left as a compliance afterthought.
  • Principle extracted. A long horizon raises the stakes on two choices: where returns are held, and whether small convex positions are owned at all. Defaults such as 60/40 need checking before they are inherited.
  • Framework implementation. A 60-to-80-year horizon makes tax treatment consequential; the framework reserves Roth for positions that may rotate. At equal tax rates in and out, Roth and pre-tax end even. For convex, right-tail positions the balance tips toward Roth because contribution limits are set in dollars, required distributions can push large pre-tax balances into higher brackets, and heirs generally inherit a Roth free of income tax under current law (Part 4). CIS (Part 6) scores each convex position on how it survives stress as well as on its upside.

Boundaries

What the framework intentionally excludes.

A lineage also says something by what it leaves out. Three well-regarded approaches sit outside this framework. None of them is wrong; each works under conditions, and the useful question is where those conditions end. If you index, trust market efficiency or buy quality and hold it, here is what the framework does differently, and why.

Jack Bogle: Passive indexing

Passive indexing (buy the market, hold it indefinitely, keep fees low) does very well in long bull markets and stable regimes. From 1980 to 2020 the S&P 500 returned about 12 percent a year with dividends reinvested, and an index fund kept nearly all of it at minimal cost. What indexing does not address is regime transitions. From 1966 to 1982 the index’s price rose only about 2.5 percent a year, and even with dividends reinvested it only about kept pace with inflation near 7 percent a year. From 2000 to 2009 it fell 49 percent and then 57 percent, and on price alone it did not hold above its 2000 high until 2013. The framework accepts more complexity to handle transitions that passive strategies were not designed for.

Eugene Fama: Efficient market hypothesis

The efficient market hypothesis captures something important: consistent alpha is rare, and most active managers trail their benchmarks after fees. What it does not fully address is reflexivity, liquidity cycles and regime transitions. A market can price current information efficiently and still misprice a structural shift that has not happened yet. Druckenmiller and Soros made their names less by exploiting persistent mispricings than by positioning ahead of regime changes the market had not priced; their 1992 bet that Britain could not keep the pound in Europe’s exchange-rate mechanism is the famous case. The framework respects efficiency for what is already known, and positions around how slowly big transitions get priced.

Charlie Munger: Quality compounders

Buying high-quality businesses at fair prices and holding them indefinitely works well for durable competitive advantages in stable environments. What it does not fully address is opportunity cost and regime exposure. A business compounding at, say, 12 percent a year is a fine thing to own; in some regimes, assets such as Bitcoin or AI infrastructure may compound much faster, which raises the cost of sitting them out. The framework respects quality but ranks convexity and regime positioning ahead of steady compounding.

Key Insight

Passive indexing does well in long bull markets, the efficient market hypothesis prevents many tactical mistakes, and quality compounders hold up through most ordinary cycles. The framework gives up some of that reliability in normal conditions to adapt better in transitions: a different objective, with different trade-offs.

Tax Architecture

Tax as a structural return multiplier.

The approaches above are ones the framework leaves out. Taxes are the opposite case: something the tradition leaves out and the framework picks up. Where a holding sits changes what it keeps, year after year, whatever your skill at picking it. None of the four, Edelman included, treats as a first-order design variable. This framework treats it as one.

Over horizons of 60 to 80 years, tax drag becomes one of the largest forces acting on terminal wealth; Part 4 and Part 5 work the arithmetic and state their assumptions.

The exhibit below holds the return fixed and changes only the tax treatment. The longer the horizon, the wider the gap.

Asset selection determines what you own; tax architecture determines how much of it you keep.

No single wrapper is best for every asset. Positions you expect to sell, rotate or rebalance gain the most from tax-free compounding, so the framework reserves Roth for them. Positions meant to be held indefinitely, borrowed against or left to heirs may do better in a taxable account, where the gain can be deferred, the holding can be pledged for a loan and, under current law, the cost basis steps up at death. Part 4 sets out the routing. The framework gives wrapper choice the same weight as risk management and convexity.

Interpretive Inputs

How the framework uses thought leaders.

Everything so far is the method, and it does not change with the news. The macro thesis does, and so do the thinkers who inform it. The framework treats them as interpretive inputs rather than authorities. They help read the structural forces behind a given thesis, but they do not set construction rules, risk limits, position sizes or wrapper routing; those stay with the lineage. When the thesis changes, the list of thinkers can change with it.

Thought leaders are selected on three criteria:

  1. Domain specificity

    demonstrated insight into one kind of force, such as regime transitions, liquidity dynamics or technological buildouts.

  2. Model coherence

    internally consistent frameworks capable of producing falsifiable implications.

  3. Instrumental utility

    the ability to translate abstract forces into signals, constraints or capital-flow pathways you can act on.

Current thesis example · illustrative, not foundational

Macro thesis thought leaders

The thinkers below inform the current example thesis only. It combines the Fourth Turning reading of history (William Strauss and Neil Howe’s 1997 book; Howe’s 2023 sequel, The Fourth Turning Is Here, dates the current crisis era from 2008 to the early 2030s) with AI infrastructure buildout, fiscal dominance and liquidity-driven asset cycles, over a 2024-to-2035 horizon. The thesis is illustrative and may be replaced as conditions change; the lineage above stays.

Ray Dalio: Regime analysis. Dalio’s regime methodology, more than his All Weather allocation, informs how the framework looks for macro-thesis opportunities. The framework reads his regime work along three dimensions: growth, inflation and policy. His debt-cycle work (Principles for Navigating Big Debt Crises, 2018) puts short-term debt cycles at about seven years, give or take three, adding up over time to long-term cycles of about 75 years, give or take 25. That gives context for policy constraints and for how fiscal dominance tends to unfold, including how deleveragings resolve. It matters most when debt is high relative to income.

Lyn Alden: Liquidity cycles. Alden’s work on fiscal dominance and liquidity cycles (M2 growth, central-bank balance sheets, real rates) helps read when the regime favors duration and speculation over safety and liquidity. Bitcoin has tended to move in the same direction as global liquidity over multi-month windows: in 83 percent of 12-month periods and 74 percent of 6-month periods from 2013 to mid-2024, and more sensitively than traditional assets over longer time frames, according to “Bitcoin: A Global Liquidity Barometer” (written by Sam Callahan, commissioned and advised by Lyn Alden, September 2024). The study measures direction, not a fixed multiple, and the link weakens over short windows. The framework expects the relationship to matter most under fiscal dominance, and it may weaken as Bitcoin matures or the monetary regime shifts.

Liquidity often decides whether a sound thesis has the force to move prices now.

Macro Thesis

Identification, evaluation, and governance.

Thought leaders feed the thesis; they are not the thesis. The framework asks you to hold a macro thesis: a coherent, falsifiable view of the structural forces likely to shape capital flows over the next 5 to 20 years. That is a different job from market timing (next quarter’s Fed decision) or sector rotation. Without a thesis, a portfolio is a list of tickers with no shared reason to exist. With one, every position has to show how it expresses the thesis, and entries and exits follow a process decided in advance instead of a mood.

A valid thesis passes four tests, and passing them is what lets you put probabilities on it and prove it wrong:

  1. Structural persistence over cyclical timing

    identify forces that persist for years, whatever the precise timing. “AI infrastructure will require massive power buildout” is structural; “chip stocks will peak next quarter” is timing.

  2. Capital flow implications, not just narrative

    specify where capital is likely to flow. “Deglobalization requires reshoring” implies flows toward domestic industrial capacity; “the world is changing” specifies no destination.

  3. Falsifiable via observable indicators

    a valid thesis can be shown wrong by events you can measure. Falsification applies to the thesis itself. A stretched valuation or a reflexive reversal does not falsify it, and a drawdown while the thesis holds is volatility.

  4. Multi-year conviction runway

    durable enough to survive the volatility that comes with transitions. Conviction in the thesis does not mean static positions: sizing and turnover answer to CIS, posture and tripwires (Part 5).

The four tests work as gates. Most stories fail at least one, which is the point of having them.

Building a thesis follows a set sequence. Each step produces an output that feeds the next, keeping the force itself apart from how it is interpreted, and both apart from how positions in it are governed.

  1. Structural force identification. Identify forces that will run for years, backed by mathematical, physical or political necessity rather than opinion. The output is a named structural thesis: a claim about what force exists and why it persists. Example: “AI infrastructure buildout will require massive power generation expansion through 2035 and beyond.” That claim should not change with market conditions.

  2. Capital flow pathway mapping. Translate the structural force into what it requires capital to build. If the thesis is AI-driven data-center buildout, capital flows to power generation, semiconductor production, networking infrastructure and data-center real estate. The output is a map of the sectors, asset classes and instruments where capital has to concentrate.

  3. Interpretive grounding. Apply thought leaders and historical analogs to refine how the thesis is read. Find the investors who came through similar transitions, take the tests they used to confirm a view, and turn their principles into characteristics you can measure. The output is a set of interpretive inputs that sharpen the reading without changing the thesis itself.

  4. Governance context. Establish the current phase of thesis expression: early structural, mid-cycle buildout or late expression. The phase is a judgment you make and record with the thesis. It informs how fast you build and how closely you review, inside the sizing bands that CIS and posture set (Part 5); it does not decide whether the thesis is valid. A thesis in late expression is still valid; it needs different handling than the same thesis early on. The dashboard stores the phase with your thesis, shows it and passes it to its AI features as context, but sizes nothing from it (as of September 2026).

A thesis becomes actionable when it finds the scarce input the rest of the system cannot easily replace.

Thesis work is iterative: refine the thesis as evidence accumulates, drop it when it is falsified, and hold it when noise creates an opportunity. The process is a method, not a forecast.

Validity and phase are separate questions. A thesis can stay right for a decade while its phase, and your judgment about how hard to press it, changes underneath.

End of Part 2

Part 2 set out the method and the thesis it serves. The method comes from Taleb, Druckenmiller, Soros and Edelman, holds whatever the regime, and adds tax treatment as a design variable none of them formalized. The thesis runs from structural force to capital flows, interpretation and phase, and it has to be falsifiable.
